match.reason: The bank point explains who First Nations entrepreneurs are and gives the Gumatj example, but it does not teach the new point's ideas of a growing sector, dual profit and community or Country goals, or government buyers seeking out these businesses.

rejected.title: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander businesses
card: An Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander business is owned by Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander people. These businesses are a growing sector and work in many industries, such as tourism, construction, food and the arts.
Like any business, they aim to earn a profit. Many also have other goals, such as supporting their community, sharing and protecting culture, and caring for Country.
Country is a word used by many First Nations people for the land, waters and sky they belong to and have a duty to look after.
Some buyers, such as governments, can choose to seek out these businesses when they need goods or services. This can help the businesses win customers and grow.
rejected.remember: These businesses seek profit and often also goals for community, culture and Country.

a.q: Which statement best describes many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander-owned businesses?
opts: They seek profit and often also community or cultural goals
They seek only cultural goals and do not need to earn profit
They are found in only one industry, such as tourism
They are run by the government and owned by the public
a.why: The card says these businesses aim for profit like any business, and many also have goals for community, culture and Country. The tempting option about cultural goals only is wrong because profit is still an aim.
a.clue: Think about what they share with any business, and what else they may add.

b.q: A state government agency needs catering for a large event. It chooses a caterer owned by Aboriginal people in Bendigo, which also trains local young people. Which describes this choice?
opts: A buyer seeking out a business with community goals
A business being forced to change its goals by a buyer
A business that has given up profit to help its community
A government agency starting its own catering business
b.why: The card says buyers such as governments can seek out these businesses. The caterer still sells a service for profit while also training young people, so it has not given up profit. The agency is a customer, not the owner.
b.clue: Who is the buyer here, and who is the seller?

version.title: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander businesses
card: An Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander business is at least half owned by Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander people. There are thousands of them, the number is growing, and they work in many industries, such as building, tourism, food, cleaning and the arts.
Like any business, they aim to earn a profit. Many also aim to help their community, such as by hiring and training local Aboriginal people, and to keep culture strong.

Many also care for Country: the land, waters and sky that First Nations people belong to and have a responsibility to look after. A business might, for example, do land care or guide visitors on Country.
Some buyers seek out these businesses. Governments in Australia have targets to buy from them, and lists help buyers find them. Winning this work helps the businesses grow.
version.remember: They aim for profit, many also work for community, culture and Country, and buyers can seek them out.

a.q: Which is true of many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander-owned businesses?
opts: They aim for profit and also for community goals
They aim for community goals instead of profit
They work in only a few industries, such as art
They are owned and run by a government agency
a.why: Like any business they aim to earn a profit, and many also aim to help their community, culture and Country. The goals sit side by side, so community goals do not replace profit.
a.clue: What do they share with any other business?

b.q: A Victorian council has a goal to buy more from Aboriginal businesses. It needs weeds cleared along a creek and picks a land care business owned by Aboriginal people, which also trains local young people. Which statement best fits?
opts: The council is a buyer seeking out an Aboriginal business
The business has given up its profit to train young people
The council now owns and runs the land care business
The law makes the business sell its work only to councils
b.why: The council is a customer choosing to buy from an Aboriginal business, as governments can. The business is paid for its work, so training young people sits alongside profit rather than replacing it. The council buys the service but does not own the business.
b.clue: Who is buying here, and who is selling?

a.best: They aim for profit and also for community goals

b.best: The council is a buyer seeking out an Aboriginal business

check.summary: No problems found. The ownership definition (at least half owned) matches the Commonwealth Indigenous Procurement Policy, though Supply Nation uses 51 per cent; the point is about First Nations peoples, so it needs the owner's review.
